title: Heavy limbs, slow machines — why proximal actuation rules robotics
figureNote: higher limb angular acceleration achieved by relocating joint motors from wrist to torso
body: Rotational inertia scales with the square of the distance from the pivot point: \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\). Placing heavy frameless motors and strain-wave gearboxes directly at the wrist or ankle quadruples the torque required to accelerate the limb. Modern high-speed robots and humanoids route power through cable capstans or four-bar linkages, concentrating actuator mass near the torso.
soWhat: Actuator packaging geometry dictates cycle times. A robot with 50% lighter distal limbs can move twice as fast with half the electrical energy.
basis: Rigid body rotational dynamics \(I = m r^2\) and motor torque-speed curves.
source: Featherstone (2008), Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms; MIT Biomimetic Robotics Lab.

title: Motors stall, they don't break — the thermal limit on physical force
figureNote: torque drop from peak rating to continuous holding torque due to winding Joule heat
body: An industrial robot holding a heavy payload motionless against gravity generates zero mechanical work output (\(W = F \cdot d = 0\)), but dissipates 100% of input electrical power as resistive \(I^2 R\) heat inside copper stator coils. Peak torque can be sustained for only 1–2 seconds before stator temperatures exceed 150 °C and insulation degrades.
soWhat: Continuous robot payload is limited by thermal dissipation, not magnetic saturation. Without liquid cooling or high-gear reduction, static holding quickly overheats actuators.
basis: First-law thermodynamics, copper resistivity temperature coefficients, and stator potting thermal resistance.
source: Kollmorgen TBM2G Thermal Whitepaper; IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics.

title: The hardest part of a robot is an elastic steel cup
figureNote: single-stage reduction ratio inside a 25 mm thin ring with zero backlash
body: Strain-wave (harmonic) gearing relies on continuously deforming a thin-walled alloy steel flexspline through an elliptical wave generator. S-shaped conjugate tooth flanks maintain simultaneous mesh across 30% of teeth. Mastering vacuum-melted ESR alloy steel cleanliness, flexspline fatigue life, and sub-micron tooth grinding took four decades of proprietary metallurgical experience.
soWhat: High-torque precision reducers are the single deepest mechanical hardware moat in robotics. Harmonic Drive Systems and Leaderdrive anchor global supply.
basis: Musser (US Patent 2,906,143), S-tooth profile patents, and ISO 6336 gear fatigue standards.
source: Harmonic Drive Systems Technical Reference Manual; Leaderdrive IPO Prospectus.

title: Vision locates the mug; only tactile touch prevents crushing it
figureNote: closed-loop tactile reflex latency required to arrest shear slip on delicate objects
body: RGB cameras and depth sensors provide macro-scale guidance (10–30 Hz), but the moment a robotic gripper touches an object, the contact interface is completely occluded from external view. Detecting incipient friction slip, micro-texture, and contact shear vectors requires high-density elastomeric tactile skins and sub-millinewton force feedback.
soWhat: Generalist manipulation without tactile sensing is fundamentally blind at the contact boundary. Vision-only policies drop slippery objects or crush fragile surfaces.
basis: Coulomb friction cone mechanics, GelSight photometric stereo reconstruction, and contact slip dynamics.
source: Johnson & Adelson (2009), Retrographic Sensing; MIT CSAIL Tactile Research.

title: Perfect in MuJoCo, broken on metal — the physics reality gap
figureNote: faster-than-realtime simulation throughput on parallel GPU physics engines
body: Physics engines simulate contact dynamics as smooth convex complementarity problems, ignoring non-linear stick-slip friction, cable stretch, backlash hysteresis, and sensor latency jitter. A neural policy trained in a static simulation fails on real metal unless domain randomization systematically perturbs physics parameters during training.
soWhat: Simulation provides scalable sample collection, but Domain Randomization and real-world system identification are non-negotiable to bridge the reality gap.
basis: Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) formulations and domain randomization statistical bounds.
source: Todorov et al. (2012), MuJoCo; Peng et al. (2018), Sim-to-Real Transfer with Domain Randomization.

title: There is no internet to scrape for physical work
figureNote: fully-loaded human cost per hour of curated real-world robotic demonstration data
body: Large Language Models pre-train on trillions of internet text tokens scraped virtually for free. Physical manipulation has no pre-existing dataset: every hour of bimanual trajectory data requires physical hardware rigs, human teleoperators, and manual environment resets. Data collection is the single most capital-intensive phase of physical AI development.
soWhat: Robotics foundation models face a severe data bottleneck. Teams with deployed robot fleets harvesting shadow-mode failure data hold a structural competitive advantage.
basis: Teleoperation economics, Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), and Open X-Embodiment datasets.
source: Zhao et al. (2023), ALOHA / Mobile ALOHA; Open X-Embodiment Consortium (2023).

title: 95% reliable is 100% unemployable in physical automation
figureNote: maximum allowable human intervention per robot-hour for profitable enterprise deployment
body: In software AI, a 95% accurate model delivers immediate value. In physical automation, a 95% success rate means an error every 20 operations (once every 3 minutes in high-speed picking). If a human supervisor must walk over or tele-operate every 3 minutes, the labor cost is not saved, only transferred. Physical automation requires 99.9%+ reliability.
soWhat: Log-odds reliability governs commercial deployment. Moving from 99% to 99.9% reliability (reducing interventions from 1/hr to 0.1/hr) creates 10× more enterprise value than moving from 90% to 99%.
basis: Queuing theory, MTBI (Mean Time Between Interventions), and warehouse labor economics.
source: Symbotic Annual Report; Covariant Logistics Case Studies; A3 Robotics Statistics.

title: Fast robots need physical cages; uncaged robots must be light and slow
figureNote: maximum permissible transient impact force under ISO/TS 15066 collaborative safety limits
body: A 100 kg industrial robot moving at 2 m/s carries over 200 Joules of kinetic energy—enough to cause fatal blunt force trauma upon impact. ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 enforce statutory speed and force limits. Robots sharing human space must either move slowly (<0.5 m/s) with compliant low-inertia joints or deploy certified 3D safety scanners that pause motion when humans approach.
soWhat: Humanoid robots operating near people cannot run at full speed without physical isolation or certified 3D dynamic speed-and-separation monitoring zones.
basis: Biomechanical pain threshold studies (Fraunhofer IFF) and ISO/TS 15066 clamping limits.

title: The cast steel outlives the software four times over
figureNote: service life of heavy cast-iron robot arms across multiple controller generations
body: Heavy cast-iron industrial robot arms (Fanuc, ABB, Yaskawa) have structural design lives exceeding 20 years with periodic bearing and grease replenishment. However, the motion controllers, edge compute boards, and AI software stacks become obsolete every 4–6 years. A thriving secondary market refits 15-year-old mechanical castings with modern digital controls.
soWhat: Hardware value depreciates slowly; software moats iterate rapidly. Robot OEMs capture long-term profit through proprietary controller retrofits and lifecycle service contracts.
basis: Weibull mechanical fatigue life curves and industrial equipment secondary market transaction data.
source: IFR World Robotics 2024; Surplus Record Machinery Database; ABB Remanufacturing Operations.
